newsitem.title: FRANCE: HORSE RACING-ARC TRENDS POINT TO HELISSIO.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-ARC TRENDS POINT TO HELISSIO.

text.p: Picking winners is never easy but trends and statistics, especially in big races, can sometimes be helpful.

In the the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe, although it may seem an over-simplification, a selection must generally have won its most recent start. Of the leading fancies, this rules out Classic Cliche, Pentire, Darazari and Shaamit.
In the last 10 years, only one horse, Subotica, has failed to meet this criteria.
But Subotica and all the winners since 1986 have had proven group one form to their credit.
Horses over the age of four have a poorish record, ruling out the five-year-old Sunshack.
When five-year-old Tony Bin obliged at odds of 14-1 in 1988, he was the first older horse to score since Star Appeal back in 1975.
French-trained runners usually win the Arc.
Lammtarra triumphed from his English base last year but in the last 10 years 60 English-trained runners have yielded just three winners.
The Irish are really up against it, with no success since Alleged's back-to-back victories for Vincent O'Brien in 1977 and 1978.
Of the French trainers, Andre Fabre is very much the man, with three Arc winners -- Trempolino, Subotica and Carnegie -- in the last 10 years.
Two of those, Trempolino and Carnegie, used the Prix Niel, held over course and distance, as the stepping stone for the Arc.
So where does this leave Sunday's Longchamp field?
There's no doubt that current favourite Helissio fits the bill very well.
Elie Lellouche's three-year-old was a smooth winner of the Prix Niel -- when reportedly only 80 percent fit -- and earlier posted group one wins in the Prix Lupin and Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud.
Dermot Weld's Zagreb was an impressive winner of the Irish Derby but has not raced since and has that long Irish losing streak against him.

Classic Cliche aims to emulate Saeed bin Suroor's success in the race last year with Lammtarra and has solid group one form. But he did not win his latest start, when beaten by Pentire in the King George VI and Queen Elizabeth Diamond Stakes at Ascot.
He has also been under a bit of a cloud after failing to sparkle in training last weekend.

Pentire, too, has tasted defeat on his most recent outing, albeit in a very unsatisfactory slowly run Prix Foy over the Arc course and distance. He finished second to Swain, who is clearly a big threat, though possibly just held by Helissio on Grand Prix de Saint Cloud form.
Helissio also has the beating of Darazari on their run in the Prix Niel.
Derby winner Shaamit has not won since Epsom and his chances would appear no better than each way.
Of the other likely British runners, Pilsudski could be a live outsider. Michael Stoute's four-year-old posted a group one victory at Baden-Baden last time and appears to have peaked for this race.
But statistics tend to suggest that Helissio will triumph, chased home by Swain, with Pilsudski possibly in third place.
